query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin, sputter‐deposited chromium nitride (CrN) coating onto boride‐based components will form an adherent, diffusion–barrier layer that significantly reduces molten–aluminum corrosion compared to uncoated boride substrates.
generation.material_initial_state: A boride-based component (as used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment) with its native microstructure and no protective surface treatment.
generation.intervention: Sputter deposition of a dense CrN coating (optionally using a thin Cr buffer layer for improved adhesion) on the surface of the boride component.
generation.conditions: Exposure to molten aluminum at temperatures near the aluminum melting point (around 660–700 °C) for periods representative of process cycles (e.g., several tens of hours) in an inert or controlled atmosphere to mimic plating conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The CrN coating, with its high ceramic hardness and chemical inertness, forms a continuous and adherent barrier that limits interdiffusion and prevents direct contact between molten aluminum and the underlying boride matrix.
generation.mechanism: By acting as a physical and chemical diffusion barrier, the CrN layer inhibits the dissolution and interfacial reactions of the boride substrate with molten aluminum. This reduces the rate of corrosion by minimizing penetration of aluminum into the component and thereby slows down the kinetics of corrosive degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under the same hot-dip conditions, CrN-coated boride components will exhibit a lower corrosion rate (e.g., reduced weight loss and limited formation of corrosion products) compared to uncoated components, leading to improved longevity in molten aluminum environments.
generation.baseline: Boride-based components without any added surface coating or protective layer.
generation.boundary: The protective effect is expected to remain valid as long as the CrN coating remains intact and adherent during exposure at temperatures up to approximately 700 °C and for periods typical of plating operations; degradation of the coating through spallation or cracking could limit performance.
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude of the corrosion rate reduction is not precisely known and will depend on the coating thickness, deposition quality, and exact molten–aluminum exposure conditions. Further optimization may be needed to ensure coating integrity under cyclical thermal and mechanical stresses.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical boride-based component samples. One set is left uncoated (baseline) while the other is coated with a sputter-deposited CrN layer (with an optional thin Cr buffer layer). Subject both sets to immersion in molten aluminum at 660–700 °C under controlled atmosphere (e.g., inert gas) for a predetermined duration (e.g., 72 hours). After exposure, evaluate the samples with weight loss measurements, optical/SEM imaging, and surface composition analysis (EDS) to assess corrosion extent.
measurements: Weight loss measurements to quantify corrosion rate
Phase and composition analysis using XRD/EDS to detect any interdiffusion or coating degradation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the CrN-coated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in corrosion rate, weight loss, or degradation of microstructural integrity compared to the uncoated baseline samples, then the hypothesis that the CrN coating improves molten aluminum corrosion resistance is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: After analyzing the shapes of the impedance diagrams, the experimental results could be fitted to an appropriate physical pattern consisting of an equivalent electrical circuit (EC). This circuit consists of several series or parallel configurations of resistors, capacitors, Warburg elements, etc. and provides the most relevant corrosion parameters of the substrate/electrolyte system. In addition, to obtain a uniform and stable protective layer, sputtering technology offers a fast deposition rate and a low-cost solution. Although the development of HEA systems has been going on for more than a decade, there are few reports on the deposition of stable protective films on HEA surfaces by conventional reactive sputtering techniques. Many studies have shown that sputter deposition of CrN film on conventional stainless steel is beneficial for its wear and corrosion resistance [,]. The CrN film deposited on the surface of 316 stainless steel has a positive effect on the friction behavior in NaCl solution and high temperature environments until heated to 550 °C []. In the tribo-corrosion test, the CrN coating layer can also remain relatively stable during the ball-on-plate sliding under various applied potentials []. As stainless steels are similar to CoCrNi-based MEAs in terms of their single FCC structure and lattice constant, this study attempts to sputter CrN film with a Cr buffer layer on the surface of CoCrNiSi0.3 MEA and discusses in detail the improvement of corrosion and wear resistance of CoCrNiSi0.3 MEA by sputtering CrN film.
